title: India-Canada Trade Deal by End of 2026 Is 'Very Realistic,' Envoy Says
excerpt: High Commissioner Chris Cooter says the political push from Prime Ministers Modi and Carney, plus strong business interest, makes the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement timeline achievable.
body:
• Canadian High Commissioner Chris Cooter has said concluding the India-Canada Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement by the end of 2026 is "very realistic."
  • His remarks follow a push from Prime Ministers Narendra Modi and Mark Carney, who reaffirmed the CEPA commitment on the sidelines of the G7 Summit in France.
  • The third round of CEPA negotiations concluded in Ottawa from July 6 to 10, 2026, with both sides reporting positive progress across negotiating tracks.
  • Canada currently has nearly $109 billion invested in India — about a quarter of its total Indo-Pacific investment — while Indian investments in Canada stand at around $11 billion.

The Deal Is Within Reach

Canada's top diplomat in India says the long-negotiated India-Canada trade deal could be concluded by the end of 2026, signaling renewed momentum in a relationship that has spent recent years repairing itself. Canadian High Commissioner to India Chris Cooter described the timeline for concluding the proposed Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) as "very realistic," underlining what he called strong political and business momentum behind the negotiations, in an interview reported by ANI.

https://x.com/CP24/status/2098082002813468689

"I think it's very realistic. There are a couple of reasons for that. Probably the most important one is that our two Prime Ministers want it to happen."

— Chris Cooter, Canadian High Commissioner to India

Cooter's remarks follow a meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on the sidelines of the G7 Summit in France, where both leaders reaffirmed their commitment to conclude CEPA talks this year. "The political will is there. We want to do this. We know we need it," Cooter said, noting that negotiations have been actively progressing over the past few months.

Context & Background

The CEPA talks have been stop-start for years, stalled by broader strains in India-Canada relations. The current push began with the Modi-Carney meeting at the G7, after which India's Ministry of External Affairs said both leaders welcomed the "positive momentum" in bilateral ties and reviewed progress in economic cooperation, including commercial arrangements related to LNG, LPG, and metallurgical coal.

The third round of negotiations took place in Ottawa from July 6 to 10, 2026, with both sides reporting positive progress across multiple negotiating tracks. A CEPA goes beyond a traditional goods-focused free trade agreement: it is expected to cover services, investment, government procurement, digital trade, and sustainable development — areas of direct relevance to the technology and services firms that anchor the India-Canada economic corridor.

On the Indian side, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal has set an ambitious target of tripling bilateral trade by 2030, a goal that would require the kind of tariff and non-tariff barrier reduction a CEPA delivers.

Impact & Analysis

The numbers behind the optimism are substantial. Cooter said Canada currently has nearly $109 billion invested in India — almost 25 percent of Canada's total investment in the Indo-Pacific region — while Indian investments in Canada stand at around $11 billion. A CEPA would lock in investor protections and market access on both sides, giving pension funds and institutions already committed to India greater confidence to expand.

"The business community wants this to happen. We have trade that is respectable. It needs to be much, much bigger," Cooter said. Indian officials appear aligned: India's Chief Economic Adviser V. Anantha Nageswaran met Cooter in New Delhi in July to discuss unlocking economic opportunities through the CEPA, deepening trade and investment ties, and driving sustainable growth.

For Indian exporters — from textiles and gems to pharmaceuticals and IT services — a deal by year-end would open a more predictable pathway into the Canadian market just as both economies seek to diversify trade partnerships in an uncertain global environment.

Diaspora Angle

The Indo-Canadian community, one of the most economically active diaspora groups in Canada, sits at the intersection of this deal. Easier movement of goods, services, and professionals would directly benefit diaspora-owned businesses that import from or export to India, while deeper investment ties mean more Canadian capital flowing into Indian markets where many diaspora investors already hold stakes. A signed CEPA would also institutionalize a relationship that the community has sustained commercially even through political turbulence.

What's Next

With the third round done and both governments reaffirming a 2026 deadline, the next negotiating round is expected to tackle the hardest remaining issues — agriculture access, services liberalization, and procurement rules. Cooter's confidence notwithstanding, trade agreements have a habit of slipping past announced deadlines, so the real test will be whether the political will from both prime ministers survives the technical fine print. If it does, the year-end signing would cap one of the fastest trade turnarounds in the bilateral relationship's history.
